Hyundai Motor Group's announcement for its brands occurred on October 5, 2023, followed by the BMW Group on October 17, 2023, and Toyota on October 19, 2023. [1, 2, 3, 12] This series of agreements signaled a significant industry shift towards a unified charging standard for electric vehicles sold in the U.S. and Canada. The adoption of NACS ports will be phased in, with Hyundai starting in the fourth quarter of 2024 for U.S. models and the first half of 2025 for Canadian models. [8] BMW and Toyota plan to begin integrating the NACS port into their new electric vehicles in 2025. [2, 3] This move will grant customers of these brands access to over 12,000 of Tesla's Superchargers across North America, with adapters being made available for existing CCS-equipped vehicles starting in early to mid-2025. [1, 2, 5] <2> Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) officially announced on September 21, 2023, that it will adopt the North American Charging Standard (NACS) for its next-generation electric vehicles starting in 2025. This agreement grants Jaguar EV drivers access to over 12,000 of Tesla's Superchargers across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. New Jaguar models released from 2025 onwards will feature an integrated NACS port, eliminating the need for an adapter. For current owners of Jaguar I-Pace vehicles, which use the Combined Charging System (CCS1) connector, Jaguar will source and supply adapters from Tesla to enable access to the Supercharger network once they are available. <3> On September 20, 2023, the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office (AMMTO) announced the selection of eight projects to receive a combined total of $2 million in funding. This initiative aims to advance the rejuvenation, recycling, remanufacturing, and reuse of lithium-ion batteries to strengthen the domestic supply chain. The projects, administered through the ReCell Center at Argonne National Laboratory, will involve Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs) between DOE National Laboratories and industry partners, requiring a 50% cost share. The selected projects have an anticipated performance period of one year and focus on areas such as developing room-temperature recycling processes, remanufacturing electrodes, recycling electrolytes, and workforce development. <4> On August 25, 2023, the United Auto Workers (UAW) announced that its members at Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis had voted by a combined 97% to authorize a strike if a new contract agreement was not reached by the September 14 deadline. The vote, a procedural step in negotiations, signaled strong member support for the union's aggressive bargaining position. A central issue in the contract talks was the industry's transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The UAW sought significant wage increases, the elimination of wage tiers, restoration of benefits lost in previous contracts, and crucially, job security and union-level wages for workers at new joint-venture EV battery plants, where pay was substantially lower than at traditional plants. The union argued that the Big Three's record profits, totaling a combined $21 billion in the first half of 2023, should translate to record contracts for the workers. <5> Electrify America announced significant changes to its pricing structure, which became effective on August 17, 2023. [1, 2, 4, 5] The announcement was first reported via customer emails on or around July 18, 2023. [6, 8, 12] The update included an increase in the monthly Pass+ subscription fee from $4 to $7, though the 25% charging discount for subscribers was maintained. [1, 2, 10, 12] A major change was the shift from a uniform national pricing model to a station-specific one, where the cost per kWh or per minute varies by location based on factors like local market conditions. [1, 4, 6] Additionally, the company reinstated idle fees, charging $0.40 per minute for vehicles that remain connected for more than ten minutes after a charging session is complete. [2, 6, 7, 10] <6> In the second quarter of 2023, the U.S. saw record sales of new battery-electric vehicles (EVs), with nearly 300,000 units sold. This represents a significant 48.4% increase compared to the same period in 2022. As a result, the market share for EVs reached 7.2% in Q2 2023, up from 5.7% a year prior. While Tesla remained the top seller of EVs, its market share fell below 60% for the first time. Cox Automotive has projected that the total number of new EVs on U.S. roads will exceed one million in 2023. One report from the Alliance for Automotive Innovation presented slightly different figures, stating nearly 355,000 EV sales in Q2 2023, a 58% increase from Q2 2022, and an EV market share of 9.1%. Despite the record sales, some analysts noted that the days of 75% year-over-year growth are likely over, and the market is facing a period of more challenging growth. <7> A report from the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), published in July 2023, found that existing and concretely announced public electric vehicle (EV) charger deployments will satisfy at least 70% of the public chargers needed in the U.S. by 2030. This analysis is based on the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposed standards for light-duty vehicles. The report further specified that for direct current fast chargers (DCFCs), the announced deployments are projected to meet more than 100% of the need beyond 2032. Since the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, announced investments total almost $22 billion, which are expected to result in over 800,000 new charger ports by 2030. If less definite commitments, such as unawarded grants and other 'soft' announcements, are included, the projected deployments could fulfill over 100% of the total required public chargers by 2030. <8> By the end of the second quarter of 2023, the U.S. electric vehicle market saw its inventory swell significantly, indicating that production was outpacing consumer demand. In late June, the days' supply for EVs peaked at over 100 days, with some reports stating 103 days, a stark contrast to the industry-wide average of about 53-56 days for all vehicles. This inventory growth was accompanied by record EV sales of nearly 300,000 units in Q2, a 48.4% increase year-over-year. The market shift led to greater competition, with manufacturers offering significant incentives and price cuts—notably by Tesla—which resulted in the average price paid for an EV dropping by nearly 20% year-over-year as of June.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On November 1, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced $44.8 million in funding for eight projects aimed at advancing electric vehicle (EV) battery recycling research. Sourced from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, this initiative is designed to lower the costs associated with recycling EV batteries and their components. The projects will focus on research, development, and demonstration of recycling and second-life applications for used EV batteries. A key objective is to enhance the recovery of critical materials, such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel, to foster a sustainable and resilient domestic supply chain for high-capacity batteries. <2> Kia America announced its best-ever October sales in company history, with a 16% increase compared to the previous record set in October 2023. This significant growth was primarily driven by strong demand for the company's electrified and SUV models. Sales of Kia's all-electric (EV) vehicles surged by 70% year-over-year. The company sold 68,908 units in the U.S. during October 2024. Several models, including the Sportage, Carnival, and EV6, set new individual sales records for the month of October. <3> In September 2024, the U.S. electric vehicle (EV) market share hit a record 9%, according to data published by Cox Automotive. This marked the sixth consecutive month that new EV sales exceeded 100,000 units. The report also noted that incentives for new EVs were substantial, with the average incentive package averaging over 12% of the vehicle's transaction price, which is significantly higher than the industry average of approximately 7%. <4> On October 11, 2024, the District of Columbia Department of Transportation (DDOT) announced the initial conditional awards for the development of four Direct Current Fast Charging (DCFC) electric vehicle charging stations. [1, 2, 3] The grants, funded by $1.34 million from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Program, were awarded to Equilon Enterprises LLC, operating as Shell Oil Products US. [1, 3] The new stations will be located along federally designated Alternative Fuel Corridors. [1] Separately, on October 22, 2024, the Puerto Rico Highway and Transportation Authority awarded contracts to four companies for the construction of a total of six charging stations. [4] <5> On September 20, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced over $3 billion in funding for 25 projects across 14 states to enhance the domestic production of advanced batteries and battery materials. This second round of funding, part of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, will support the retrofitting, expansion, and construction of new facilities for processing critical minerals, manufacturing battery components, and recycling. The initiative is designed to strengthen the U.S. supply chain, reduce reliance on China, and is expected to create over 8,000 construction and 4,000 operational jobs. Notable recipients of the grants include Honeywell International Inc., which will receive approximately $126.6 million to build a facility in Louisiana for producing a critical electrolyte salt for lithium batteries. Other major awardees include Albemarle, The Dow Chemical Co., and Form Energy, with projects covering a range of technologies from lithium-ion to iron-air batteries. <6> According to data from S&P Global Mobility, new electric vehicle (EV) registrations in the United States increased by 18% in July 2024 compared to the same month in the previous year, totaling 118,273 units. [1, 4] This growth, which ended a five-month slump for market leader Tesla, was significantly driven by new models, particularly the Tesla Cybertruck and the Honda Prologue. [1] In July, 5,175 Cybertrucks were registered, a figure that nearly matched the 5,546 combined registrations of all other electric pickup models. [1, 3] An analyst from S&P Global Mobility noted that generous incentives were a key factor in the sales surge, making EVs more price-competitive with internal combustion vehicles. [1, 4] Despite Tesla's overall market leadership, its share of new EV registrations fell to 48% from 56% a year prior, while non-Tesla EV registrations grew by 38%, indicating rising competition. [4] <7> On September 11, 2024, the California Energy Commission (CEC) and the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) announced the award of over $32 million in federal funds from the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program. This initial round of funding, part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, will support the installation, operation, and maintenance of 458 direct-current fast chargers (DCFC) at 70 sites along California's major transportation corridors. Nine projects were selected in this first phase, with companies like Electrify America, LLC and Skychargers, LLC receiving significant portions of the funds. The NEVI program requires that these charging stations be located no more than 50 miles apart on freeways and highways and within one mile of an exit. California expects to receive a total of $384 million from the NEVI program over several years to further expand its electric vehicle charging network. <8> On August 27, 2024, the Biden-Harris Administration announced $521 million in grants for the continued expansion of the national electric vehicle (EV) charging and alternative-fueling network. The funding, made possible by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law's Charging and Fueling Infrastructure (CFI) Discretionary Grant Program, will support the installation of over 9,200 EV charging ports. The grants will be distributed across 51 projects in 29 states, eight Federally Recognized Tribes, and the District of Columbia. This initiative is part of the administration's goal to create a convenient and reliable national network of EV chargers and aligns with the Justice40 Initiative, as over half of the funding is directed towards sites in disadvantaged communities. The investment includes $321 million for 41 community projects and $200 million for 10 corridor fast-charging projects. The announcement noted that the number of publicly available EV chargers in the U.S. has doubled to over 192,000 since the start of the administration.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Lucid Motors, autonomous vehicle startup Nuro, and Uber Technologies have announced a partnership for a premium global robotaxi program. [6, 7] The collaboration aims to deploy 20,000 or more self-driving Lucid Gravity SUVs, equipped with Nuro's Level 4 autonomous Nuro Driver technology, over a six-year period. [4, 7] These vehicles will be owned and operated by Uber or its third-party partners and will be available exclusively on the Uber ride-hailing platform. [7] The initial launch is planned for an unannounced major U.S. city in 2026. [1, 4] As part of the agreement, Uber plans to make multi-hundred-million dollar investments in both Lucid and Nuro. [3, 7] A prototype of the Lucid-Nuro robotaxi is already undergoing autonomous testing at Nuro's facility in Las Vegas. [5, 7] <2> During the second quarter of 2025, the United States recorded its second-largest quarterly growth in high-speed public charging infrastructure, with the addition of 703 new stations. This expansion increased the national total to approximately 11,400 fast-charging stations. Notably, this growth extended into rural areas, and nearly two-thirds of the new stations were installed in states that do not have a zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. <3> In a report published on July 14, 2025, Cox Automotive detailed the U.S. new electric vehicle market for the second quarter of 2025, which concluded on June 30, 2025. The report indicated that new EV sales decreased by 6.3% year-over-year, with a total of 310,839 units sold. Despite the annual decline, sales showed a 4.9% increase compared to the first quarter of 2025. Cumulatively, total EV sales for the first half of the year reached a record 607,089 units. Cox Automotive anticipates a significant sales surge in the third quarter, predicting it will likely be a record, before a potential collapse in the fourth quarter. This forecast is linked to the expiration of government-backed tax incentives of up to $7,500, which are set to end on October 1. <4> Cox Automotive has predicted that the third quarter of 2025 will likely see record Electric Vehicle (EV) sales. This surge is anticipated to be driven by a rush of buyers aiming to capitalize on the federal tax credit of up to $7,500 for new, qualified EVs before it expires. Following this peak, Cox Automotive forecasts a potential sales collapse or a likely decline in the fourth quarter of 2025 as the market adjusts to the absence of the incentive. The federal tax credit is set to phase out on October 1, 2025. <5> A report from Cox Automotive's Kelley Blue Book, published on July 14, 2025, revealed that new electric vehicle sales in the U.S. for the second quarter of 2025, ending June 30, 2025, decreased by 6.3% year-over-year. A total of 310,839 new EVs were sold during this period. However, these figures showed a 4.9% increase from the first quarter of 2025. The first half of the year set a sales record with 607,089 total EV sales, which is a 1.5% increase compared to the first half of 2024. <6> A Q2 2025 automotive recall report from BizzyCar, which analyzes data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), indicated a sharp increase in U.S. vehicle recalls. Between April and June 2025, a total of 7,322,767 vehicles were recalled, a figure that more than doubled the volume from Q1 2025 and marked the highest quarterly total since Q1 2024. Ford Motor Company led all manufacturers with 3.3 million vehicles recalled across 49 campaigns, accounting for nearly half of all vehicles affected. The leading issue was 'Back-Over Prevention,' impacting 2.59 million vehicles from various automakers, and included recalls for rearview camera displays on models like the Ford Mustang Mach-E. Other significant recall categories included engine and cooling systems (1.14 million vehicles) and hydraulic service brakes (775,000 vehicles). Notably, 94.6% of the recalled vehicles had defects posing a risk of crash or injury, and the quarter saw three 'Do Not Drive' and three 'Park Outside' advisories. <7> The United Auto Workers (UAW) has filed multiple unfair labor practice (ULP) complaints against BlueOval SK, a joint venture between Ford Motor Co. and SK On, at its battery plants in Glendale, Kentucky. A UAW press release from July 1, 2025, announced a call for the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to investigate the company for alleged illegal union-busting activities before scheduling a union election. The complaints, numbering six in total by July 2025, accuse BlueOval SK of threatening, restraining, and coercing workers. Specific allegations include the destruction of union materials, threatening to close the facility, and firing workers for supporting the union. The union contends that the company's actions, which allegedly include holding mandatory anti-union meetings, have created an atmosphere of fear that prevents a fair election. These charges are part of a broader unionization effort that began with workers filing for a union election in January 2025, citing concerns over safety, benefits, and pay. <8> In April 2025, new electric vehicle registrations in the U.S. fell by 4.4% to 97,833 units, marking the first time registrations have dropped after 14 consecutive months of growth. [9] This resulted in electric vehicles accounting for a 6.6% share of the total market, which is down from the 7.4% share they held in April 2024. [9] <9> On May 30, 2025, Toyota announced a major step in its electric vehicle strategy, confirming plans to manufacture two new all-electric vehicle models in the United States. Production is scheduled to begin in 2025, with one EV model to be built at its Georgetown, Kentucky, facility—the company's largest plant globally—and a second model at its plant in Princeton, Indiana. This move is part of a broader company initiative to offer seven distinct EV models in the U.S. by the middle of 2027.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In July 2025, the Trump administration enacted a series of policy changes designed to slow the adoption of electric vehicles in the United States. [1] Key measures included the termination of federal purchase incentives for new and used EVs, which will take effect on September 30, and the complete shutdown of the national charging infrastructure program. [1] Furthermore, the administration revoked California's legal authority to enforce its own zero-emission vehicle mandate and imposed significant tariffs on imported electric vehicles and related auto parts. [1] <2> General Motors and Hyundai Motor Company announced a significant strategic collaboration on August 6, 2025, to co-develop five new vehicles for the Americas. This partnership, which builds on a framework agreement signed in September 2024, aims to leverage the companies' combined scale to reduce costs and accelerate vehicle delivery to customers. The plan includes four models for Central and South American markets—a compact SUV, a compact car, a compact pickup, and a mid-size pickup—with flexible internal combustion or hybrid powertrains. A key component of the agreement is the joint development of a new all-electric commercial van specifically for the North American market, which is described as a smaller counterpart to Chevrolet's existing BrightDrop vans. Hyundai will lead the development of the compact vehicles and the electric van, while GM will head the development of the mid-size truck platform. The companies will maintain their distinct brand identities with unique interior and exterior designs despite sharing common platforms. Production of the new vehicles is scheduled to begin in 2028, with the electric van set to be manufactured in the United States. <3> The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the IRS announced that since January 1, 2024, American consumers have saved over $2 billion on the purchase of more than 300,000 clean vehicles through a point-of-sale rebate program established by the Inflation Reduction Act. This program allows car buyers to transfer their clean vehicle tax credit, worth up to $7,500 for new vehicles and $4,000 for used ones, directly to a registered dealer, which reduces the vehicle's price at the time of purchase. The option to transfer the credit to the dealer became effective on January 1, 2024. The announcement of the $2 billion milestone was made on August 6, 2025, and highlighted that of the 300,000 advance payments issued, over 250,000 were for new clean vehicles. This initiative is designed to make electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles more affordable and accessible, saving consumers from having to wait to claim the credit on their tax returns. <4> A Carvana EV Trends Report for the second quarter of 2025 confirmed that electrified vehicles (EVs and PHEVs) accounted for a record 9% of the company's total unit sales, a significant increase from just over 2% in Q2 2023. The report highlights a major shift in consumer preference, with SUVs becoming the dominant body style for electrified purchases, representing nearly 44% of EV and PHEV sales, up from 24% in the same quarter of 2023. Tesla models secured the top three spots for pure EVs, with the Model 3, Model Y, and Model S leading sales. In the PHEV category, Jeep models were the most popular, with the Wrangler Unlimited 4Xe, Wrangler 4Xe, and Grand Cherokee 4Xe comprising the top three sellers. The report attributes the overall growth to a substantial increase in vehicle selection, with Carvana offering 66% more EV models and double the PHEV options compared to two years prior. <5> On June 30, 2025, Volkswagen Group made a $1 billion equity investment in Rivian as part of a larger potential agreement worth up to $5.8 billion for a technology joint venture. [1, 8, 10] In its second-quarter financial results announcement on August 5, 2025, Rivian confirmed the investment and also reported that its vehicle production had been limited. [1, 8] The production constraints for both R1 products and commercial vans were attributed primarily to various supply chain complexities, which were partly influenced by shifts in trade policy. [1, 7, 13] <6> General Motors announced record U.S. electric vehicle sales for July 2025, selling more than 19,000 EVs, which represents an increase of over 115% year-over-year. [1] The sales were driven by the Chevrolet Equinox EV, which sold over 8,500 units, marking its most successful sales month ever in the United States. [1] <7> Hyundai Motor America announced its best-ever July sales, with total sales for July 2025 reaching 79,543 units, a 15% increase compared to July 2024. [1, 5] The company's retail sales also saw an 18% climb to 73,064 units. [1, 2] Fueling this growth was a significant 50% jump in electrified vehicle sales, which constituted nearly a third of the retail mix. [1, 3] The IONIQ 5 had its best sales month ever, with a 71% increase in retail sales, amounting to 5,818 units sold. [1, 3, 4] In addition to the IONIQ 5, Hyundai also set new all-time monthly sales records for the Elantra HEV, Elantra N, Santa Fe HEV, Palisade, and the Santa Fe family. [1, 2, 5] <8> Ford announced a net loss of $36 million for the second quarter of 2025, marking its first quarterly loss since 2023. The loss was attributed to costs associated with a field service action and the cancellation of a battery-electric vehicle program. Compounding the financial challenges, Ford raised its projected tariff costs for the year to $3 billion, an increase of $500 million from the previous forecast of $2.5 billion. This significant hit from tariffs erased the company's net profit, despite strong sales in its electrified vehicle segment. <9> The California Energy Commission announced that 100,671 zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) were sold in California during the second quarter of 2025. These sales represented 21.6% of all new vehicles sold in the state during that period. This milestone pushed the total number of cumulative ZEV sales in California to over 2.3 million.

This surge contributed to a 19% increase in the nation's fast-charging infrastructure during the first nine months of the year. The growth was significantly driven by retail and restaurant chains aiming to attract EV drivers. Notable contributors included Target with 14 new stations, Wawa with 12, Cracker Barrel with six, and both Ikea and Dunkin' with four each. Pilot Travel Centers was also a key player, activating 27 new stations during the quarter. This expiration also applied to the 45W leasing credit, worth up to $7,500. The termination of these credits was a direct result of the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' (OBBBA), which was passed in July 2025 and significantly moved up the original expiration deadline from 2032. In anticipation of the deadline, electric vehicle sales saw a notable surge, with an increase of 17.7% in August. Analysts expect this consumer pull-forward effect to lead to a slowdown in EV sales following the expiration of the credits. <3> In August 2025, the U.S. electric vehicle market achieved its highest-ever monthly sales, a surge attributed to consumers purchasing vehicles before the federal tax credits expired on September 30, 2025. Sales surpassed 175,000 units, pushing the EV market share to a record high of 9.9%. This consumer rush was in response to the termination of the up to $7,500 new and $4,000 used EV tax credits, a change resulting from President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which significantly shortened the credits' original 2032 timeline. Amidst this market-wide boom, several automakers reported record EV sales, including General Motors, which sold over 21,000 battery-electric vehicles. <4> In July 2025, the Trump administration enacted a series of policy changes designed to slow the adoption of electric vehicles in the United States. [1] Key measures included the termination of federal purchase incentives for new and used EVs, which will take effect on September 30, and the complete shutdown of the national charging infrastructure program. [1] Furthermore, the administration revoked California's legal authority to enforce its own zero-emission vehicle mandate and imposed significant tariffs on imported electric vehicles and related auto parts. [1] <5> General Motors and Hyundai Motor Company announced a significant strategic collaboration on August 6, 2025, to co-develop five new vehicles for the Americas. This partnership, which builds on a framework agreement signed in September 2024, aims to leverage the companies' combined scale to reduce costs and accelerate vehicle delivery to customers. The plan includes four models for Central and South American markets—a compact SUV, a compact car, a compact pickup, and a mid-size pickup—with flexible internal combustion or hybrid powertrains. A key component of the agreement is the joint development of a new all-electric commercial van specifically for the North American market, which is described as a smaller counterpart to Chevrolet's existing BrightDrop vans. Hyundai will lead the development of the compact vehicles and the electric van, while GM will head the development of the mid-size truck platform. The companies will maintain their distinct brand identities with unique interior and exterior designs despite sharing common platforms. Production of the new vehicles is scheduled to begin in 2028, with the electric van set to be manufactured in the United States. <6> The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the IRS announced that since January 1, 2024, American consumers have saved over $2 billion on the purchase of more than 300,000 clean vehicles through a point-of-sale rebate program established by the Inflation Reduction Act. This program allows car buyers to transfer their clean vehicle tax credit, worth up to $7,500 for new vehicles and $4,000 for used ones, directly to a registered dealer, which reduces the vehicle's price at the time of purchase. The option to transfer the credit to the dealer became effective on January 1, 2024. The announcement of the $2 billion milestone was made on August 6, 2025, and highlighted that of the 300,000 advance payments issued, over 250,000 were for new clean vehicles. This initiative is designed to make electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles more affordable and accessible, saving consumers from having to wait to claim the credit on their tax returns. <7> A Carvana EV Trends Report for the second quarter of 2025 confirmed that electrified vehicles (EVs and PHEVs) accounted for a record 9% of the company's total unit sales, a significant increase from just over 2% in Q2 2023. The report highlights a major shift in consumer preference, with SUVs becoming the dominant body style for electrified purchases, representing nearly 44% of EV and PHEV sales, up from 24% in the same quarter of 2023. Tesla models secured the top three spots for pure EVs, with the Model 3, Model Y, and Model S leading sales. In the PHEV category, Jeep models were the most popular, with the Wrangler Unlimited 4Xe, Wrangler 4Xe, and Grand Cherokee 4Xe comprising the top three sellers. The report attributes the overall growth to a substantial increase in vehicle selection, with Carvana offering 66% more EV models and double the PHEV options compared to two years prior. <8> On June 30, 2025, Volkswagen Group made a $1 billion equity investment in Rivian as part of a larger potential agreement worth up to $5.8 billion for a technology joint venture. [1, 8, 10] In its second-quarter financial results announcement on August 5, 2025, Rivian confirmed the investment and also reported that its vehicle production had been limited. [1, 8] The production constraints for both R1 products and commercial vans were attributed primarily to various supply chain complexities, which were partly influenced by shifts in trade policy. [1, 7, 13] <9> General Motors announced record U.S. electric vehicle sales for July 2025, selling more than 19,000 EVs, which represents an increase of over 115% year-over-year. [1] The sales were driven by the Chevrolet Equinox EV, which sold over 8,500 units, marking its most successful sales month ever in the United States. [1] <10> On August 1, 2025, S&P Global Mobility released its forecast anticipating a modest increase in U.S. light vehicle sales for July 2025. The projection estimated a sales volume of 1.33 million units, translating to a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of 15.9 million units. This expected rise was primarily attributed to a surge in battery-electric vehicle (BEV) purchases as consumers sought to buy before the federal EV tax incentives expire on September 30, 2025. S&P Global Mobility projected that the BEV market share for July would exceed 9%, a notable increase from the 7.3% average earlier in the year.
